item.content:encoded:
Frankie Muniz isn’t racing away from his struggles.
The Malcolm in the Middle actor got candid about what he’s been going through over the last six weeks, admitting his life has felt like “a nightmare I’m praying to wake up from.”
“Everything felt heavy, unclear, and like it was falling apart at the same time,” Muniz posted on X Sept. 18. “I wouldn’t wish this season on anyone.”
The admission comes over two months after he and wife Paige Price—with whom he shares 5-year-old son Mauz Mosley Muniz—announced their divorce after six years of marriage.
Still, there is a silver lining for the 40-year-old, as he explained, “The unexpected gift in the middle of it is that I’ve had nowhere to hide. I’ve had time to sit with myself, do real self-reflection, and finally see the areas of my life that need work if I want to become a better version of me. Not the polished version I show the world...the actual one.”
Muniz said he recently read that "sometimes hitting rock bottom is the thing that wakes you up" and becomes a catalyst to force “the changes you needed to make all along so you can live the best life possible.”
And that idea stayed with the race car driver, who imagined in five years time he will “look back at this exact low point and feel grateful for it,” especially because getting to a better place in his life necessitated going through the difficulty.
“This isn’t the end of the story. It’s the part where I start doing the work...the uncomfortable, unglamorous, necessary work. I’m choosing to treat this season as the foundation, not the finish line,” Muniz wrote. “If you’re in a low place right now too, you’re not broken. You’re being rebuilt. Let's keep going!”
In recent weeks, Muniz has been open about the difficult time he’s been facing, posting on X Aug. 26, “Am I naive to say that I didn't know that having a broken heart actually meant your heart physically aches. I'd rather break my back again.”
On Sept. 1 he wrote, “Struggling,” and a few days later on Sept. 6 shared two photos of himself as a child, captioning the pictures, “Sometimes I wish I could go back to this.”
For more stars who have been candid about their own struggles, keep reading.

item.title: [E! News] Gwyneth Paltrow Reveals the Real Story Behind Her and Chris Martin’s “Conscious Uncoupling”

item.content:encoded:
Gwyneth Paltrow and Chris Martin consciously uncoupled for their kids.
The Oscar winner revealed that she and the Coldplay frontman made a very specific decision to keep their focus on kids Apple, 22, and Moses, 20, as they announced their separation in 2014, which lead to their now infamous declaration of “conscious uncoupling” after 10 years of marriage.
“We really sat down and thought, ‘Is there a way that we could do this?’ Paltrow shared on a recent episode of the Friends Keep Secrets podcast. “Because—this is very me—but when I was getting divorced, I was like, ‘How do I do this?’”
The question led the 53-year-old to her friends who grew up with divorced parents, as she asked what the most difficult part was for them.
“I said, ‘Tell me what was the worst thing. What do you feel you have scars from to this day?’” she explained. “And they said, ‘You know, it wasn't really so much the divorce, ‘cause you're a kid, and yes, of course, the idea of it is terrible, but you sort of get used to that quickly.’”
In reality, the most difficult part for most of them was the tension they felt between their parents during and after the divorce.
“‘My dad used to drop me off at the end of the driveway. It was so tense at my birthday parties. They never ate dinner in the same room until my college graduation and it caused me so much pain,’” Paltrow recalled of her friends’ experiences. “So I was like, ‘How could we not do that?’ Is there a way where you can sort of circumvent all of that awful stuff when no one is in the same room and get to the graduation where you're all having dinner at the same table.”
The conversation was helped by Paltrow and Martin’s therapist at the time, who introduced them to the concept of conscious uncoupling and making “a commitment to really put the kids first” and to “stay a family even though we weren't a couple.”
Still, despite coming into it with the best of intentions, the two experienced their share of stressful situations that they did their best to diffuse.
“We used to have brunch every Sunday, the four of us,” Paltrow shared of one such time. “I remember—it’s early on in the thing—and Chris and I were upset with each other about something.”
But the Goop founder didn’t want to let the day “go really off the rails,” so as soon as she and Martin felt the tension begin, they stepped away to the front porch.
“We’re like, ‘Let's just not. Let's just not,’” she said. “We just hugged and we're OK. We fist bumped and then we went to brunch.”
And while Paltrow—who married Brad Falchuk in 2018—is certainly grateful for how she and Martin handled their divorce, she can also understand why there was a bit of backlash to them using the phrase and the way they described their breakup at the time.
“Say you had a really nasty divorce and then you hear this idea that, ‘It doesn’t have to be done this way,” she explained on Good Hang With Amy Poehler in January. “I think implicit learning is like, ‘Oh, f--k. They’re saying I did something wrong.’ Which, of course, was not the intention, but that makes sense to me. That's not a nice thing to contemplate, so I do understand why it was so personal for people.”
